articles.title: Do you think teachers are similar to coaches, pastors or something else? It depends on where you live
articles.author: Gustavo E. Fischman, Professor of Education Policies and Comparative Studies, Arizona State University
paras: Three answers, three countries, one open-ended question: “Teaching is similar to what other occupation or activity?”
We asked this question to more than 3,000 people across the United States, England and Australia between May 2025 and March 2026.
Coaching was the front-runner across all three countries. But the similarities partially diverged there.

Respondents in England and Australia more often compared teaching with professional roles such as nursing and social work. U.S. respondents, meanwhile, more often likened teaching to being a parent and religious roles, such as a cleric or pastor.
In the three countries, however, one other idea stood out: Teaching was primarily associated with a caring relationship.
We have previously examined how Republicans and Democrats in the U.S. find common ground on what makes a good teacher, despite the polarization in the country on education and many other issues.
This time, we wanted to know whether people across countries had similar ideas of teachers.

In all three countries, respondents most often described teaching as centered in the relationship between teacher and student: a form of coaching, caregiving, parenting and other types of personal support.
Coaching was the most common answer in each country, but its prominence varied.
Coaching was named by 30% of U.S. respondents, compared with 23% in England and 23% in Australia.
The differences became more pronounced when participants named other occupations and activities.
Respondents in England and Australia were more likely to associate teaching with institutional, credentialed and paid professional roles, such as nursing, lecturing and social work.

“Nursing. They care for and look after people whilst they are at their most vulnerable. Teachers do a similar thing by caring and teaching young people some of the skills they will need later in life,” a 39-year-old Australian man told us.
“A lecturer, you are passing on knowledge to people, usually the younger generation,” another 32-year-old man in England said.

Compared with respondents in those countries, U.S. respondents were more likely to describe teaching through caregiving roles, such as parenting, and through religious figures, such as priests, pastors or rabbis.
“Being a parent, you are caring for young minds and shaping them through learning,” a 33-year-old woman in the U.S. told us.
“As a preacher, he teaches the word of God. How they deliver the word determines how well the people will understand it,” a 23-year-old woman in the U.S. said.

While international comparisons are informative, they do not represent a single view of teaching. Instead, they suggest that respondents in three countries likely drew on somewhat different cultural repertoires when describing the profession.
We were surprised by just how much agreement we found.

Despite differences in schooling models and cultural norms, people in the United States, England and Australia had remarkably similar ideas about how relationships are at the heart of teaching, closely echoing our other work showing that Republicans and Democrats view teachers similarly.
AI is not at the center of people’s thinking
In September 2026, The New York Times conducted an informal survey of 37 education researchers who gave 30 ideas about how to fix schools.

Their list consists primarily of interventions such as more per-pupil funding, banning cellphones and restricting artificial intelligence in the classroom. These ideas appeared far less often in our participants’ explanations of what teaching resembles.
In fact, out of more than 3,000 responses to our survey, AI came up only a handful of times and never as the reason teaching and another occupation were said to be alike.
Given how central AI has become to political and academic debates about the future of education, its near-total absence in these public descriptions of teaching is notable.
At the same time, experts and citizens agree that what separates very good teaching from poor execution is likely the quality of the relationship between educators and children.

We think that serious conversation about student achievement must include clear descriptions of very good teachers: the practices they use to encourage and enable students to learn. Our research shows that teaching should make room for both the transmission of knowledge and the meaningful and caring relationships that make learning possible.

articles.title: What colleges and universities need from donors to thrive
articles.author: William Blomquist, Professor Emeritus of Political Science, Indiana University
paras: In 1638, John Harvard, an English-born Puritan minister and teacher in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, bequeathed 400 books and half his £779 estate, today equivalent to roughly US$2 million, to the college that would be renamed in his honor after his death.

In addition to launching America’s oldest university, Harvard’s donation began a tradition of philanthropy for U.S. colleges and universities that has continued ever since. Today, philanthropy is an important source of higher education funding that covers an average of 10% of college and university budgets.

Based on our decades of experience as scholars, academic administrators and school fundraisers, we believe that donors – and not just big ones – are especially important to colleges and universities in tough times.

Since January 2025, the Trump administration has targeted colleges and universities with research funding cuts, student financial aid caps and new restrictions on how long international students can stay in the United States.

University endowments have been in the crosshairs since the first Trump administration’s 2017 tax reform package. The big 2025 tax-and-spending package Trump signed raised the taxes on some schools’ endowments. A rule the Trump administration proposed in September 2026 would threaten private schools’ tax-exempt status if any of their programs use race-based criteria.
There are demographic problems too. Fewer students are choosing to go to college, and the number of high school graduates who could attend is falling due to a declining birthrate.
Although colleges and universities are providing more financial aid than ever, students and their families are still struggling to pay for college.

Some schools are being forced to close their doors. Sixteen colleges shut down in 2025 alone, including Indiana’s only predominantly Black college, Martin University, and ecologically focused Sterling College in Vermont.
And at least 40 colleges have been acquired by other schools since 2020, including Marymount Manhattan College and Mills College, which are now part of Northeastern University’s global network.
Donors contributed $79 billion to colleges and universities in 2025, up 4% in constant dollars from the year before.
The richest Americans dominate giving to higher education: 89% of the funds raised came from only 2% of donors in 2025.

Also in 2025, Phil and Penny Knight, the Nike co-founder and his wife, made what was then the largest single gift to a university in history when they gave the Oregon Health & Science University $2 billion for cancer research.
On Sept. 30, 2026, investor Ken Griffin broke that record by giving Carnegie Mellon University more than $3 billion to build a new campus in Miami and meet some other priorities.

It’s hardly the only megagift a university has received in 2026: Michael and Susan Dell, whose fortune comes from his computer hardware company, gave the University of Texas at Austin $750 million for its medical center. The Knights gave $1 billion to the University of Oregon for a new engineering college. Software billionaire David Duffield pledged $371 million to Cornell University. And many other schools have drawn gifts in excess of $100 million.

The vast majority of these huge gifts are reserved for specific purposes. The share of totally unrestricted gifts to colleges and universities, those given with no strings attached, has been dwindling for decades. In 2024 it slipped below 7%. Unrestricted giving did pick up somewhat in 2025. Perhaps that was a sign that some donors were responding to federal funding cuts with their gifts.

In an article in Change: The Magazine of Higher Learning in September 2026, we listed ideas for college and university fundraising efforts. These tie to three recommendations for donors – and not only those making multimillion-dollar gifts.
Donations to colleges and universities don’t have to end in lots of zeros to make a big difference.

In 2015, the grassroots Saving Sweet Briar campaign kept the small women’s college operating even after its trustees had voted to close it. The largest gift the rural Virginia school received was $2 million, and the smallest was $1.50 from a graduate’s grandchild. This is the exception rather than the rule. Financial pressures were too much for Hampshire College, a New England private college that is slated to close after the fall semester of 2026, to withstand – even with a fundraising campaign and $5 million gift from alum and documentary filmmaker Ken Burns.

Giving Days are high-profile fundraising campaigns through which many alumni and other supporters raise millions. For example, Oregon State University Dam Proud Day 2026 drew 12,400 gifts and raised over $4.1 million. Purdue University’s annual “day of giving” has generated nearly $500 million over the past decade. In 2024, it garnered $76 million from 32,000 donors.
2. Donating with few or no strings attached
Donations with few restrictions or none at all help colleges and universities meet their greatest needs.
Even if they’re mostly intended for a new building or to fund a particular program, large gifts can also include unrestricted portions to help cover costs as needs arise and priorities change.

Brandeis University, Indiana University, Princeton University and other schools encourage unrestricted annual gifts. These flexible funds are helping to cover research funding shortfalls at Cornell University, undergraduate scholarships at Georgetown University and general operations at the College of the Atlantic.

Novelist and philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, the former wife of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, has given more than $26 billion in unrestricted donations to nonprofits, including to colleges and universities. Historically Black colleges and universities as well as other schools with diverse student bodies, such as Robeson Community College in rural North Carolina, Oklahoma’s Carl Albert State College and Wisconsin’s Fond du Lac Tribal and Community College, have received Scott’s big gifts.

In 1920, the trustees of Berea College, a private liberal arts school in Kentucky, passed a resolution placing future unrestricted bequests, donations made through people’s estates, in the school’s endowment. Berea students do not pay for tuition, fees, housing or food – thanks in large part to those unrestricted donations.
3. Helping students afford all college costs so they can graduate
Supporting students directly helps them go to college, stay in school and graduate.

Donors already make gifts that fund schools’ financial aid packages, with about $7 billion in gifts designated for this purpose in 2025. But the colleges and universities that receive the most dollars from donors serve a small fraction of the nation’s undergraduate students – and not those from low-income families. We recommend that donors consider making gifts to the thousands of colleges and universities, including community colleges, that don’t typically draw big donations and have endowments totaling in the millions, rather than billions, of dollars.

Sometimes it takes more than tuition scholarships for students to graduate. Donors can pay for additional expenses, such as transportation and textbooks, and fund extra academic advising and mentoring. Billionaire philanthropists John and Laura Arnold’s Commit2Completion grant program at Arizona’s Maricopa Community Colleges addresses those kinds of often overlooked priorities.

You don’t have to be very wealthy to fund scholarships. Anyone can pitch in through platforms like Dollars for Scholars. This program’s more than 400 chapters enable local donors to pool their gifts to help students raised in their communities pay college expenses. For example, a rural Minnesota chapter awarded $248,000 to 65 college-bound students in 2025.

There are also hundreds of other place-based “promise programs” that provide tuition and fees scholarships to public colleges and universities in their areas and offer programming such as college readiness workshops and access to local employers.

Philanthropy can’t solve every problem higher education faces. But by giving together, donating with fewer strings attached and helping students pay their college expenses, alumni and other donors can be strategic in how they help.
Genevieve Shaker has received funding from the TIAA Institute and the AFP Foundation for Philanthropy.

articles.title: Why faculty diversity at universities still lags far behind the changing demographics of college students
articles.author: Rodney Coates, Professor of Critical Race and Ethnic Studies, Miami University
paras: U.S. colleges and universities have long struggled to increase the racial diversity of their faculty.

And after they are hired, some faculty of color say they feel that their qualifications and scholarship are subjected to greater scrutiny, or that they do not feel valued by their colleagues and schools.

As a scholar of critical race theory, I have studied these barriers, and I think that it is helpful to understand what universities, students and academic research all stand to gain from a more diverse faculty.
While college faculties have become more racially diverse since the 1970s, the diversification of the faculty has not kept pace with changes in the college student population.
Overall, approximately 16% of the U.S. population were of color in 1970.
In 1975, approximately 8% of full-time faculty at U.S. colleges and universities were people of color. Approximately 4% were Black, 2% were Asian, and 1% were Hispanic.
In 1976, meanwhile, nearly 16% of U.S. college students were people of color.
Black students specifically accounted for about 9% of all full-time college students in 1976, Hispanic students about 4% and Asian or Pacific Islander students about 2%.

By 2022, 72% of full-time faculty across universities and colleges nationwide were white, while Asian professors made up 13%, Black professors 7% and Hispanic professors 6%, according to the National Center for Education Statistics.
By 2022, Hispanic students accounted for 21.5% of U.S.-resident students at colleges and universities, Black students 13.2% and Asian students 7.8%.
Overall, in 2022, people of color made up approximately 41% of the U.S. population.
Diversifying college faculties has not been a straightforward journey in recent years.
After a white police officer shot and killed Michael Brown, a Black teenager living in Ferguson, Missouri, in 2014, student protests erupted across college campuses.
Amid this student activism around racism, some U.S. research universities publicly committed to making their faculties more diverse.
By 2015, at least 88 of the country’s 187 leading research universities had promised to take this step.
Another 96 schools made similar commitments over the next few years, including after the 2020 police murder of George Floyd, a Black man living in Minneapolis.
Among a group of selected research universities examined by The Washington Post, the share of Black, Hispanic and other underrepresented faculty rose from 9% in 2015 to 12% in 2024.

But many of those public efforts have since been scaled back or abandoned. Of the 184 universities that had made faculty-diversity commitments, at least 108 had fully or partially rolled them back by early 2026.

Separately, in 2023, more than 45 bills meant to restrict or ban diversity, equity and inclusion efforts in higher education were introduced in state legislatures. By late that year, eight states had enacted anti-DEI laws.
These measures have included restrictions on schools’ DEI offices and programs, diversity statements and spending on DEI-related initiatives.
Some scholars argue that these policies, along with other restrictions on racial-equity programs and initiatives, are contributing to what they describe as the “resegregation” of higher education.

Some faculty of color have said that they have seen evidence of a kind of tokenism in higher education. Some feel that they are expected to represent, exemplify, teach and do research with a focus on race and ethnic studies programs.

“Apparently, my colleague had assumed that because I am Black, I must be an expert on the African diaspora,” wrote Tyler Austin Harper, a former environmental studies professor at Bates College, in an August 2026 article in The Atlantic, which detailed his decision to leave his tenure-track position.

“The school’s culture encouraged us to see professors of color as vehicles for achieving the college’s diversity goals. The inescapable conclusion I arrived at was that I had been hired to be visibly Black first and a scholar second, if at all,” Harper wrote.
Other faculty of color have reported feeling like they and their scholarship are undervalued by their schools and peers.
Some faculty of color also report that scholarship focusing on marginalized populations or social problems is treated as less rigorous or less central to their disciplines.
Faculty of color across American colleges and universities face other challenges, including feeling isolated or like they are being watched.
Some faculty of color also report feeling like they should mentor students of color. This work can add to their workloads and, they say, sometimes come at a cost to their own careers.
Some research has found racial disparities in tenure and promotion outcomes, although those disparities vary considerably by discipline, school, gender and racial or ethnic group.
LGBTQ+ faculty of color, in particular, also report feeling isolated or intimidated, and experiencing delayed tenure or other promotion opportunities.
A diverse faculty benefits everyone
Having diverse faculty can benefit students and universities in several ways.
Research has linked greater faculty diversity to a range of positive outcomes for students, including student retention and college completion, particularly for Black and Hispanic students.
Exposure to professors with different backgrounds and perspectives can broaden students’ educational experiences.
Having a diverse faculty at universities can also strengthen academic research.
Researchers’ backgrounds can influence the questions they ask, the populations they study and how participants respond to them.
More diverse research teams can also bring different experiences and perspectives to the design and interpretation of research.

Research teams and study populations that lack diversity can overlook important perspectives and produce findings that are less applicable to broader populations. Conversely, more diverse teams can bring a wider range of perspectives and approaches to research.
I believe that continuing to make university faculty ranks more diverse is essential for higher education.

This is not simply a matter of making professors more closely resemble the students they teach. It is about broadening the perspectives represented in classrooms and research, and ensuring that universities draw on the widest possible pool of scholars and ideas.

articles.title: Students from military families are often misunderstood in US public schools – a retired military officer and behavioral health expert explains what schools can do
articles.author: Nikki R Wooten, Associate Professor of Social Work, University of South Carolina
paras: Over 1.4 million children had a parent or caregiver who served in the U.S. armed forces in 2024.
Among active-duty families, 2.4% of military children had both parents serving in the military. Another 4% lived in single-parent households.

More than 90% of these children attend U.S. public schools. Over 67,000 attend Department of Defense schools located in the U.S. and foreign countries. Military-connected students have a unique set of experiences and academic and emotional needs, including support with school transitions and developing a sense of belonging at their new school.
Because only 6% of Americans have served in the U.S. military, some educators may not understand the experiences of military children and the challenges of military life.
As a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel and military behavioral health expert, I think there are a few key ways that school districts can better support these students through school transitions.
Some strategies include identifying military-connected students during enrollment and training educators about military life.
Benefits and drawbacks of military life
The military lifestyle creates both unique opportunities and challenges for children and teenagers whose parents are military service members.

Military children often travel and have opportunities to live in multiple cities across the U.S. and other countries. They are also exposed to different cultures, new traditions and opportunities to learn foreign languages.

These children are resilient and adaptable. They may also display increased independence, personal growth and pride because of their parent’s military service. Many are thriving in school because of these traits.
Military children are also twice as likely to serve in the military as their civilian peers.
But military life can also be stressful for children.

Many children with parents in the military move frequently. They often live in more cities and attend more schools than their civilian peers – an average of two schools during high school, and for most, six to nine different schools between kindergarten and 12th grade.
They experience their parent being away from home for various periods of time, ranging from a few weeks at a time to a year or more.
They also fear that their parent might be hurt or killed while serving in the military.

As a result, military children and teenagers may experience social withdrawal, angry outbursts and mental health problems, including depression and anxiety. These challenges might also cause them to miss school, struggle to complete school assignments and have difficulty making new friends.

Recent research found that military-connected students were more likely to be disengaged in school and repeat a grade than their civilian peers. Other studies found that multiple parental deployments and longer parental separations affected children negatively. Examples include greater family stress and behavioral problems.

Children’s responses to military life vary, depending on how old they are and their level of maturity. Children 5 and younger often have limited language skills to express their feelings. As a result, they may act out behaviorally in response to changes in caregivers and daily routines.
Elementary school students may have tantrums, be clingy, have toileting accidents, engage in uncontrollable crying or become less talkative as a result of changes in schools, homes and caregivers.
Middle school students and preteens, ages 8 to 13, are likely aware of how their lives are different from their civilian peers.

These students may have experienced multiple moves and attended multiple schools over their relatively short lives. They may respond to changes in schools and household routines with angry outbursts, irritability, anxiety and social withdrawal.
They may also have fluctuating grades, peer conflict, problems completing their homework and disciplinary problems at school.
Boys and girls may express their stress differently. Boys may exhibit more anger and aggression, whereas girls might demonstrate sadness, depression and self-harm.
Military adolescents and high school students, typically 14-18, have heightened risk for anxiety, depression and suicide due to military-related stressors, especially during parental deployments.

They may experience mood changes, anger and social withdrawal. They may also disengage from school activities, perform poorly in school and choose to skip classes. Many are also high achievers despite the challenges of military life.
Military adolescents are also at risk for substance use.
My prior research from 2019 found that military adolescents had frequent emergency department visits and hospitalizations for substance use problems during the Afghanistan and Iraq wars.
How schools can support military-connected students
Military-connected students transitioning to a new school often need help early in the process to ensure they have adjusted well to their new school.

As a licensed clinical social worker and former child therapist for military children, I think brief check-ins with a school counselor or social worker are necessary to identify concerns early. These check-ins can help avoid behavioral or academic difficulties and prevent a problem from becoming worse.
U.S. public schools are required to identify students with an active duty military parent, typically by asking about military affiliation during enrollment.
Some school districts also include children of veterans and those with parents in the National Guard and Reserves in these records.
Research has consistently shown that the impact of military life continues after parents leave military service.
An estimated 2.3 million children under 18 reside with a veteran who is disabled. These children often assume caregiving responsibilities for siblings and their veteran parent.
Identifying schools that support military-connected students

State education departments can give schools a Purple Star School designation, indicating that the school is committed to assisting with the academic, social and emotional needs of military-connected students. These schools maintain a list of military students, help students with school transitions and train school personnel about the challenges of military life.
Currently, there are over 4,100 Purple Star Schools in 44 states across the U.S.

The proportion of military-connected students in U.S. public schools depends on the military and veteran population of each state and school district, as well as the geographical location of military installations.
Texas, California, Florida, North Carolina, Georgia, South Carolina and Virginia rank among the 10 states with the most military families that have children attending public schools.

Schools can help military-connected children and their families by creating a welcoming school climate, maintaining open communication with students and parents, and developing student groups and peer-support programs.

Frequent school guidance counselor, nurse or social worker visits may also be needed. High schools can develop peer-mentoring programs and suicide prevention, mental health awareness and anti-stigma campaigns.
I think it is also important for schools not to rush to identify behaviors as a disciplinary problem when family stress is the root cause.

Although military-connected students face unique challenges to success in school, I think schools should intervene early and often to meet their needs. Helping these students ensures every child has an equal chance to succeed in school.

Nikki R. Wooten, PhD, LISW-CP previously received research funding from the National Institute on Drug Abuse. Dr. Wooten retired as a lieutenant colonel from the U. S. Army after over 33 years of military service. articles.title: AI can help with academic research but doesn’t always get it right – here are some tips to check the information you receive
articles.author: Allison Faix, Librarian and Instruction Coordinator, Coastal Carolina University
paras: Almost 25% of adults in the United States are using artificial intelligence chatbots on a daily basis, a 2026 Pew Research Center study found.
At the same time, another recent study found that 48% of the information that popular free chatbots gave in response to questions about the news contained errors.
As librarians, we know that if students are using AI chatbots to help with their academic research, they shouldn’t assume that the information they’re given is accurate.
Not all AI is the same. Here are four steps we recommend to question information AI generates, including by checking the original source and considering issues that aren’t always easy to spot.
First, we think it makes sense to spend time choosing the right AI tool for the task at hand.

AI tools – be it ExLibris’ Primo Research Assistant, Research Solutions’ Scite, Anthropic’s Claude or OpenAI’s ChatGPT – are trained with various datasets and use different algorithms to generate results. They should not be used interchangeably.
Some tools might be better or worse at answering specific kinds of questions, and the types of answers they generate can vary.
People might choose ChatGPT, for example, at the beginning of their research process, because it can provide overviews and summaries to help with understanding concepts.
In subsequent stages, they might choose a tool such as Primo Research Assistant or Scopus AI, which can help find and examine peer-reviewed research that has been vetted by academics.

Students conducting academic research could also see whether their library subscribes to an artificial intelligence tool like LeapSpace or Concensus, which draw their data from peer-reviewed, scholarly research.
Using these specific AI tools doesn’t eliminate the need to evaluate their answers, but it provides more certainty that the data has gone through a review process.

Tools such as Anthropic’s Claude, meanwhile, may also draw from academic research, but to what extent is unclear. According to Anthropic, Claude states that it is trained on a proprietary mix of publicly available information from online sources, public and private datasets, user data and synthetic data generated by other models.
Finally, it can be helpful to read librarians’ reviews about AI tools to help select the best fit. People can also take a simple online test such as ROBOT to help them consider which tool to use.
Second, asking follow-up questions is an important part of evaluating the answers AI tools generate. Even if the answer an AI tool gives sounds good, it is useful to take time to learn more about it.

Checking one’s own emotions is also important, because AI chatbots have been known to flatter users by giving answers based on the user’s own biases, or what the user wants to hear, rather than just facts.

Ask the AI to tell you where it got the information, how confident it is that the answer is correct and what might be missing. Ask the AI why it believes the answer is correct, or ask it to explain how it came up with an answer.

It’s helpful to also make sure your prompt is phrased in a neutral way. For example, asking “What does psychological research say about social media and anxiety?” rather than “Tell me why social media causes anxiety” may produce different responses.
Third, it is useful to trace any claims the AI chatbot makes to their original sources.
Students may be familiar with using the SIFT process to evaluate websites. This process asks people to stop, investigate the source, find better coverage and trace claims to their original source.
Start by asking the chatbot to cite its sources, if it did not do that already.

Then, go to each source and read enough to figure out whether the AI is using the information in the right context. Also, look into who authored the source and whether they have expertise in the topic. If the AI won’t cite the sources it used, or if the sources it cites don’t include the information it said they did, pull out any claims it is making and do further research.

Can you find other, credible sources that back up what the AI is saying, using Google or a library database? Can you figure out where the AI may have gotten the information and whether that source is credible?
If this seems like a lot of work, you could always go directly to library databases instead of using AI tools.
4. Not all issues are easy to spot
Fourth, there are other, less visible issues that can play out when using AI tools.
For example, it might not always be easy to tell whether an AI tool is missing important perspectives or is giving biased information.

Remember that you, not the AI tool, are the researcher. It might be easy to rely on an AI tool to generate a summary of important sources, but deciding for yourself what sources to use helps you learn about a topic more deeply.

Research shows that most AI tools focus on sources such as websites, internet forums and other online content that is freely available and written in English. Consider what expert knowledge might be missing from AI datasets and seek out those viewpoints when needed.
Last, remember that you need to cite the AI tool you used if you are quoting or paraphrasing text generated by it in your work, just as you would cite any other source.
Artificial intelligence is changing fast. As librarians, we think it is important to continually evaluate whether the tools you are using are still working for you.
These tips are a good place to start to help sharpen your evaluation skills.

articles.title: Why it’s more important than ever to jump-start entrepreneurial careers from the college classroom
articles.author: Raghupathy Sivakumar, Vice President of Commercialization and Chief Commercialization Officer, Georgia Institute of Technology
paras: Recent college graduates are facing a job market that’s only getting tougher. Their unemployment rate hit 5.7%, compared to 4.1% for all workers, in June 2026. That may not sound like much, but it’s one of the worst rates in the past 20 years.
Meanwhile, roughly 4 in 10 graduates are underemployed, which means they work in jobs that typically don’t require a college degree. That’s the highest rate since the COVID-19 pandemic.

As an educator for more than 25 years, I see the growing anxiety every day. In a change from years past, parents are now peppering me with questions: How can their kids leverage their college education in such a fast-changing world? Will they learn skills in school that will soon be antiquated once they graduate?

What’s essential to understand is that technology adoption cycles have accelerated at a breathtaking rate over the past few years. While the telephone and television took decades to reach 100 million users, ChatGPT and TikTok attained that threshold in a matter of months. Colleges need to adapt their curricula accordingly.

Georgia Tech, where I teach engineering, has focused on pushing entrepreneurship across our campus since 2014. We’re seeing encouraging signs from our follow-ups with graduating students that it’s helping their early careers.

I believe one of the best ways to adjust to these changes is to embed entrepreneurial experiences throughout college. Such hands-on learning, in turn, develops versatile, adaptable talent, producing graduates who can pivot across jobs as industries, technologies and opportunities evolve. And this needn’t be confined to business students – young people in all majors can benefit.

The educational value of entrepreneurship isn’t principally that every student will be able to start a company. It’s that entrepreneurial experiences develop the capabilities students need in a rapidly changing economy – and ultimately build more resilient careers.
Here are some ways educators can future-proof the college experience, based on what I’ve learned and applied at Georgia Tech.

Making adaptability a core skill: Students need to learn how to be nimble. This means recognizing important changes in the landscape, identifying new problems and the opportunities they create, articulating a response and mobilizing the necessary resources. Ultimately, this approach will help students be prepared for the real world.

To impart these lessons, I believe colleges should provide hands-on opportunities to help students learn through experience before they enter the workforce. For example, they could encourage students to develop a business venture idea that addresses a newly created opportunity in the marketplace through accelerators, or short-term “boot camps” for young companies to help them grown quickly. One example is Greptile, a startup that came out of the Georgia Tech CREATE-X accelerator.
The goal isn’t that a startup will be launched – that depends on several factors coming together – but that the student gains the experience to understand a changing landscape.

Understanding customer value: Colleges can also teach students how to think about customer value – namely, why the solution they’re working on matters to the consumers buying it. This isn’t just for business students. All students can gain from learning to think about the customers or clients they will deal with in their careers. In fact, students from 38 majors have participated in the entrepreneurship programs at Georgia Tech.

Through on-the-ground experience that requires them to find customers, students can learn about the real-world impact of the products and services they create. When students spend hundreds of hours selling their young startup to the outside world, they learn to understand value at a deep level.

Emphasizing fundamentals: Fundamental skills are key because they outlast the technology underpinning the business. In fact, the more quickly specific technologies change, the more important a strong grounding in fundamentals becomes. This means it’s a smarter investment to offer, say, a fundamental course on wireless networking or deep learning concepts over a course that teaches specific wireless technologies or emphasizes the use of a specific model. A strong foundation gives students the tools to adapt to technologies that may not yet exist when they graduate.
The many paths toward entrepreneurship
Another great advantage of entrepreneurial experiences is that they force students to deal with uncertainty, recognize opportunities, work around resource constraints and learn how to create value.

But other strategies work as well. A few examples are project-based learning, internships and interdisciplinary capstone classes that let students pursue independent research projects as their final course.

That said, entrepreneurial experiences provide an unusually concentrated and effective environment that requires students to solve problems, engage with customers and mobilize resources they don’t directly control – all while getting real-world feedback.

More and more universities and colleges understand this point and have ramped up support for entrepreneurial activity for their students, such as Cornell and the University of Washington. At Georgia Tech, we have a playbook that we have developed through our experiences that follows the following principles:

Embed entrepreneurship into the curriculum: One simple way for colleges to incorporate entrepreneurial experiences into their coursework is to offer an entrepreneurship minor to all students, regardless of major. This would offer the opportunity to a broader range of students who otherwise might miss out.

Build a pathway to business creation: Entrepreneurial education is most effective when it leads to something bigger. To that end, many colleges are now offering a startup accelerator, including MIT, Rice University and the University of Texas.

But more is needed: A startup pathway that caters to students at all stages can substantially broaden participation and impact, regardless of whether a business results. At Georgia Tech, we have a learn/make/launch/scale pathway that offers programs and resources for learning about entrepreneurship, building solutions, launching new ventures and eventually scaling them.

Offer real venture experience: A successful model combines theoretical learning with hands-on experience. The confidence that students gain through that experience may be at least as important an educational outcome as the viability of the startups they launch. After all, since most startups tend to fail, confidence is a value that successful entrepreneurs have to sustain.
Transferring skills to the workforce

There’s another important element that’s needed: private sector partnerships. Fortunately, entrepreneurial education is well aligned with the interests of universities’ traditional corporate partners.

These companies, especially those with established, successful business models, are eager to hire students with a strong understanding of fundamentals and entrepreneurial confidence. This next generation can help the companies navigate the future.

Companies can also offer industry know-how, mentorship opportunities and financial and in-kind support. And they understand that students building a startup have to think beyond their own discipline to succeed. For example, an engineering student will need to understand customers, pricing, finance, sales, operations, intellectual property and team building. That broader perspective can make them more effective when they enter a corporate environment full time.

The same capabilities can also translate into venture creation itself: The value of entrepreneurial education can be seen across both traditional workforce pathways and startup outcomes. Our experience at Georgia Tech offers evidence of both.

Startups launched by Georgia Tech students over the past decade have crossed US$4.5 billion in aggregate total valuation and have created thousands of jobs. We’ve also found encouraging early evidence that students who gain confidence through these experiences have stronger career outcomes.

Georgia Tech isn’t alone. The University System of Georgia has recently created a new role: a chief innovation and entrepreneurial strategies officer to lead an initiative across all of the state’s public colleges and universities.

Other universities are pursuing similar paths, including the University of Virginia, Rice University and Cornell University. All now have an institutionwide leadership position focused on entrepreneurship.

Taken together, these developments suggest that educators increasingly view entrepreneurship as more than just support for students who want to start companies. These steps will help ensure that when students walk across the stage to receive their diplomas, they can meet the challenges ahead of them.

articles.title: Cornell 7 case puts a spotlight on fraternity misconduct – and the limits of universities’ power to stop it
articles.author: Pietro A. Sasso, Associate Professor of Education, Old Dominion University
paras: Universities have been trying for years to cut back on the abuses among fraternities, with limited resources and limited success.
A new lawsuit, filed by a former Cornell University student in September 2026, is now rattling higher education and drawing national attention.
The person, identified as Jane Doe, has alleged that seven Chi Phi fraternity members drugged and gang-raped her at an on-campus fraternity house when she was a sophomore in 2024.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten declined to pursue criminal charges against the fraternity members in 2024. Following the filing of the case and emergence of new information, however, Van Houten said on Sept. 26 that he is planning “to discuss new evidence that exists” with the former Cornell student about her sexual assault claims.

The high-profile Cornell case is just one of the latest fraternity scandals. In August 2026, Pennsylvania announced charges against current and former Penn State fraternity members for their involvement in a criminal narcotics operation.

As an education scholar who researches the experiences of undergraduate college students and fraternities, I believe that universities and colleges have not devoted enough resources toward curtailing the hazing, sexual assault and other kinds of dangerous behavior that sometimes happens at fraternities or other student organizations.
But there is only so much they can do – in part because beneath it all is a hypermasculine culture of proving one’s worth.
A need for more enforcement
In 1984, the National Minimum Drinking Age Act pressured states to set 21 as the minimum age to purchase and consume alcohol. All states made 21 the minimum age by 1988.
The change meant that most college students could no longer legally purchase alcohol, leading some of them to drink in more private settings, like fraternity houses.
Some universities felt concerned about the alcohol-related injuries and deaths occurring at fraternity houses. Schools also faced the possibility of lawsuits over underage drinking.

Harmful binge drinking remained a major problem on college campuses throughout the 1990s and early 2000s. A lot of the documented hazing incidents at fraternities during this time also involved alcohol.
Sexual assault on college campuses, including at fraternities, was another major issue during this time.

A lot of universities started to respond to students’ excessive alcohol use, in part through social norming. This term means correcting people’s mistaken beliefs about what their peers normally do, like regularly drinking excessively.

They also tried other harm-reduction strategies, like sharing direct information with students about the negative effects of consuming alcohol, as well as peer-led interventions to try to reduce unsafe drinking or encourage alcohol moderation.
But they didn’t necessarily respond to related problems surrounding hazing, such as substance misuse or addiction.

Some of the students’ parents, including those who had children who died as a result of hazing, were concerned. They developed a large, nationwide parent lobby to advocate for changes in hazing laws across states. These groups, not the universities, have been the most influential in advocating for changes in hazing laws.

It’s not that some universities haven’t tried to reduce hazing on their campuses. These efforts include practices such as hosting educational sessions, workshops, speakers and even placing moratoriums on social fraternity events that include alcohol.
Recent approaches have included teaching students how to recognize when their peers are emotionally distressed and need help.

Some universities have started research centers on hazing or hired full-time staff members whose jobs involve prevention and response work following a harmful incident such as hazing or sexual violence.
Universities can kick fraternities off campus and kick out athletes who are charged with hazing or sexual assault.

But fraternities can also exist as private organizations, independent of a university. A university can withdraw recognition from a fraternity chapter and prohibit it from hosting events on campus, but that does not necessarily prevent the organization from hosting gatherings off campus.

Another issue is that universities and colleges like Cornell have a civil process for dealing with hazing and other crimes, including sexual assault, but not a criminal one. Schools cannot launch a criminal investigation, but they can levy educational sanctions, including banning students from campus or taking away students’ scholarships.
Expelling students for illegal misconduct such as sexual assault and hazing is a really common approach, but that is about as far as these schools can go in terms of discipline.

Schools may also cooperate with criminal investigations. Campus police, for example, can share their evidence and records with outside law enforcement. Or university staff may testify against students in court. But universities themselves cannot bring criminal charges.
After Jane Doe reported the incident to university police, Cornell says it took action.

In a September 2026 statement, Cornell said its range of sanctions included “expulsions and suspensions.” A few students were asked to write essays, but Cornell says this wasn’t “as a sole consequence of their involvement.”
The Chi Phi chapter involved in the incident was also closed in 2024, according to Cornell.
Following the lawsuit and recent national attention it received, Cornell agreed to bring in outside lawyers to determine whether it properly conducted the 2024 rape investigation.
Proving your masculinity can become a central part of proving your worth and fit at a fraternity.
This hypermasculine culture – combined with a culture of secrecy – could be a powder keg for sexual violence. It’s a dynamic also seen in the military and on sports teams.
Hypermasculinity is not simply tied up in an individual’s behavior, but can become embedded within organizational cultures that reward toughness, dominance, risk-taking and silence.
In fraternities, these expectations may shape how members understand belonging and status. These issues may also discourage students from expressing vulnerability and seeking help.

Understanding these gendered and cultural dynamics is, I believe, essential to developing prevention efforts that address not only individual conduct, but also the organizational norms that allow harmful behaviors to persist.

articles.title: How Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library is helping kids start reading when they’re very young
articles.author: Alex H. Poole, Associate Professor of Information Science, Drexel University
paras: By the time Dolly Parton died on Aug. 25, 2026, her Imagination Library had gifted more than 332 million children’s books to babies and kids in all 50 states and four other countries: Canada, the U.K., Australia and Ireland.
If they were set end to end, these books would circle the earth 1.8 times.

This free program mails an age-appropriate book monthly to each enrolled child from birth to age 5, meaning up to 60 books will fill these children’s shelves by the time they graduate from the program.

Though a selection committee tweaks the lists annually, each participant receives Watty Piper’s “The Little Engine That Could” as their first book and Nancy Carlson’s “Look Out Kindergarten, Here I Come!” as their last.

I’m an information science professor who studies reading behavior. In my research for an upcoming academic article about the Imagination Library, I’ve found that its free monthly books help families develop children’s literacy, prepare children for kindergarten and encourage a lifelong love of reading.
Emphasis on early literacy

Parton, most remembered as a popular country singer, embraced many musical genres during her long and successful career in show business. She was also a songwriter, entrepreneur, actor and philanthropist.

She created this program because she, like most early childhood literacy experts, believed that reading begins in the home. That is, parents and other guardians are a child’s first teachers, and reading aloud to children contributes to their future literacy.
First graders who struggle with reading usually continue to have trouble with literacy later on.

Very young children in lower-income households generally have less access to books and hear fewer words than higher-income kids. This class-based difference may lead to disparities in reading skills later on.

Like Parton, who was born in a one-bedroom cabin in an Appalachian region of Tennessee that had neither running water nor electricity, the Imagination Library’s origins were modest. It started in her hometown, hardscrabble Sevier County, in late 1995. Its initial order of 1,760 books was destined for the children who lived where she grew up.
The program came from “a very serious place in my heart,” Parton once said. On many occasions, she emphasized how her own father’s illiteracy inspired her to found it – with him.

“Daddy couldn’t read nor write, and it always just seemed to cripple him, and he was embarrassed about it,” Parton told American Libraries in 2018. “My daddy just loved it when all the little kids would call me ‘The Book Lady,’” she said later.

In contrast, Parton was a bookworm. “I always loved books,” she explained in an interview. “I don’t remember learning to read, it was just something I always did. That’s how I knew there was a world beyond the Smoky Mountains.”
Parton’s Dollywood Foundation covers overhead and administrative expenses, coordinates the book selection committee, maintains the book order system and arranges orders and fulfillment.
The Imagination Library is available to any child in a community participating in the program, regardless of their family’s income.

To be eligible, a community must secure a local partner. Local partners publicize the program and enroll children. They have to pay US$2.60 per month per child to defray costs of purchasing books wholesale and mailing them. These partners include schools, public libraries and government agencies, and several kinds of nonprofits, including foundations.
Nonpartisan expert committees of educators and librarians select the books, nearly all published by Penguin Random House.

The program is continuing under the direction of the Dollywood Foundation’s president, Jeff Conyers. A Penguin Random House vice president said, “We will continue that work with the utmost pride and care, just as we know she would have wanted.”
But funding challenges have arisen in at least four states.
Steady growth and diversification

By 2001, the Imagination Library had expanded to affiliates in nearly a dozen states. The next year, it extended its reach to 92 Native American communities, partnering with the Cherokee Nation, the Bureau of Indian Affairs, Parents as Teachers and the National Center for Family Literacy.
In late 2003, the Imagination Library mailed its one-millionth book. In 2004, it launched its first statewide program – fittingly, in Tennessee.

It added bilingual titles in Spanish and English in 2003 and launched a bilingual Spanish website in 2022. The Imagination Library also supplied audio and braille books for those who needed them beginning in 2011.

Parton celebrated when the library mailed its 100-millionth book in 2018. “We never thought it would be this big,” she told NPR. “I just wanted to do something great for my dad and for my home county and, at the most, maybe a couple of counties over. But then it just took wings of its own.”

The Imagination Library shipped its 200-millionth book in 2023 and its 300-millionth book in 2025. By 2024, 1 in 7 children under the age of 5 in the United States were receiving books for free every month, courtesy of this initiative.

Other programs give free books to young children, including Reach Out and Read in the U.S., which since 1989 has handed them out at children’s medical checkups. Bookstart, which launched in 1992, offers every baby in England, Wales and Northern Ireland a free book and tips on reading aloud to kids.
Parents and caregivers highly praise the program.
Many studies have found that children get excited about getting their own books in the mail, addressed to them personally. Both they and their families also take great pride in book ownership.
“A lot of (children) wait at the mailbox at the first of the month,” Parton told The Washington Post. “They think that I bring the book myself, like I’m Santa Claus.”
As one parent told an education researcher, “We read the books when they come in the mail instead of watching TV.”

The library’s books “nudge” children to make reading a regular habit. Many studies have found that children who are read to more frequently by their loved ones, spend more time reading together daily and ask more frequently for books to be read to them.

This program aims not only to boost a child’s love of reading but to improve their cognitive development and get them ready for elementary school by enlarging their vocabulary and improving their listening skills.

Kids who get the books tend to know more letters, understand how books and printed words work, recognize and retain words’ sounds, and both understand and use more spoken words. Similarly, children enrolled in the program have scored higher than their peers when they take a standard kindergarten entrance early-reading skills test.
In line with Parton’s original goal, the Imagination Library may do the most to change reading habits in lower-income homes – where children’s books tend to be scarce.

articles.title: Using an AI chatbot to practice new languages can be helpful, but it doesn’t replace speaking with an actual person
articles.author: Antonio Perez-Nunez, Associate Professor of Spanish, College of Charleston
paras: Approximately 30% of U.S. adults who were learning a language in 2025 reported that they were using artificial intelligence as a resource.

People can use AI-powered chatbots, like ChatGPT and Gemini, to practice conversations in other languages, ask what an unfamiliar phrase means or get feedback on their writing. These apps and websites also offer voice features for speaking and listening in another language.
But can someone learn a language with a chatbot alone?
Research suggests that these tools can help learners build language skills, but there isn’t evidence that strictly using these apps is enough to become fluent in another language.
That said, they can still offer a helping hand. Learning another language involves understanding what you hear and read, as well as knowing how to express yourself verbally and in writing.
I study how chatbots can help someone practice these four skills in different ways.
What learners can gain from chatbots depends on how they use them.
Chatbots can help build language proficiency

First, people can use the voice features in chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini to role-play conversations and practice speaking about different topics. People can practice for a job interview by answering questions about their experience, asking for feedback and trying different ways of expressing an unfamiliar phrase.

Research suggests that practicing speaking with chatbots can help language learners become more fluent and accurate. People can repeat a conversation and try again after receiving feedback from the chatbot, giving them time and perhaps the confidence to work on unfamiliar expressions and recurring mistakes.

Speaking another language can be stressful, especially when people worry about making mistakes in front of someone else. Some language learners report finding chatbot conversations less intimidating than interactions with people, and feeling they can experiment without worrying about being judged.
Not being self-conscious may make people more willing to speak and keep practicing after they make a mistake.

Chatbots can also support people as they draft a sentence or a paragraph in another language, and offer them feedback and revisions. Research suggests that these tools can help identify grammar errors and improve sentence structure and clarity. Immediate feedback can also encourage learners to revise more often.

But the quality of the feedback that chatbots offer varies. A review of 51 studies on AI feedback in second-language writing found that this kind of feedback could contain errors or misinterpret the writer’s intended meaning. Some studies also reported that learners relied too heavily on AI, taking less control over decisions about their own writing.

Chatbots work best, then, when learners consider which individual suggestions to use and why. For example, they can check whether a suggested change preserves their intended meaning, or ask a chatbot why it was recommended and try using what they learned from the feedback in a new sentence.

People could also ask a voice-enabled chatbot to tell a short story or ask questions, then request that it repeat or rephrase anything they do not understand. In a study of university students in China, language learners practiced listening with ChatGPT and received feedback on their answers outside their regular English classes. Their English listening test scores improved more than those of students who used teacher-provided materials for that additional practice.

Finally, chatbots can help someone work through difficult reading material in a foreign language. Research suggests that reading a simplified version first may help learners grasp the main idea and work out unfamiliar words.
Chatbots can help people develop some language skills, but they still lack the cultural understanding, lived experience and emotional support that actual human beings bring to a conversation.
For starters, chatbots may reflect cultural biases.

A study of 10 language models compared their answers about the importance of work and religion, among other values, with human survey responses. The chatbots’ answers were generally closer to those of people from the Netherlands, Germany, the United States and Japan, even when asked to respond as someone from India or China.

Some responses also relied on stereotypes. Asked to imagine an ideal job for a Dutch person, Gemini suggested leading bicycle tours past cheese factories, windmills and tulip fields. For language learners, this raises concerns that a chatbot may provide cultural information that is inaccurate, biased or oversimplified.

Privacy matters, too. Companies providing chatbot services may record learners’ text and voice data. Practicing a job interview with real details about an employer, for example, could involve sharing confidential information with a chatbot.
In a survey published in 2025, students who reported more positive experiences with chatbots also worried more about feeling disconnected from other people and lacking emotional support.

In language learning, a 2026 study of 10 English teachers and 10 students at a university in Turkey explored their experiences using AI in the classroom. Some found it useful for teaching and learning, but their accounts also emphasized the importance of connecting with people.

Existing research on using chatbots to learn a language also has limits. Studies in one review tested activities lasting from a single learning session to about four months of practice. Most studies involve adults, and English is by far the most studied language.
Longer studies involving different ages of learners and an array of languages would help establish whether the benefits last and how widely they apply.

As chatbots become more widely used, educators can help students evaluate their responses and make their own decisions about how to use them. For example, a teacher might ask students to write a draft, get feedback from a chatbot and explain why they accepted, adapted or rejected its suggestions.
Teachers also build relationships based on trust and an understanding of students’ needs. They might talk through a difficult task with a discouraged student and offer encouragement to keep going.

Teachers need training to make effective use of chatbots. This includes understanding how they work, recognizing their limitations and learning to design and select activities that meet students’ learning needs.

Chatbots offer new ways to practice a language and build skills, but the evidence does not yet show that they are enough on their own. For now, their clearest value may be offering new opportunities to learn alongside teachers and other speakers.
Antonio Perez-Nunez is the owner of Lingua Innova LLC. Outside of academia, he developed a chatbot-based platform for conversation practice that is owned by Vista Higher Learning.

articles.title: Why Trump’s plan to cut Head Start regulations could undermine services for the country’s poorest families
articles.author: Alexander Thim, PhD Candidate of Economics, UMass Amherst; Westfield State University
paras: For over 60 years, the federal program Head Start has helped children from low-income families get ready for elementary school through early childhood education and related support services, like speech therapy and developmental screenings.

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced on Aug. 6, 2026, proposed changes that would cut the majority of the rules that guide Head Start programs and would also give states more authority over how the federal program is run.

This proposal comes after the Trump administration tried unsuccessfully to defund Head Start in 2025. Funding freezes and the government shutdown in 2025 also caused many Head Start centers to temporarily close. These closures caused some staff to resign and compelled some Head Start families to withdraw their children from the program.

The latest proposed changes could alter the program’s day-to-day operations in various ways – whether that means no longer giving children free daily meals or relaxing the program’s student-to-teacher ratio requirements.
The new rules would also mandate that all classes be taught in English, regardless of the language children and their families speak at home.

Some Head Start participants, workers and advocates have expressed concern that these changes would transform Head Start into a different program – from one that alleviates the effects of poverty to one that has a more generic emphasis on early childhood education.
As a doctoral candidate in economics, I’ve spent the past six years studying Head Start and its impact on local communities.

Head Start is a vital provider of childcare and other services for the poorest children and their families in rural, urban and suburban communities across the U.S. Reducing the number of federal rules governing Head Start will likely not enhance the quality or broaden the availability of the program to the children and families who need it most.
Understanding Head Start’s launch

Head Start is a free, nationwide year-round preschool program that serves more than 700,000 low-income children ages 3-5 and their families. It operates with a US$12.3 billion annual budget. Head Start providers are typically run by nonprofits or local schools.

Eligibility for the program is generally determined based on household income, though there are some categories of children who are automatically eligible, such those who are unhoused or in foster care.
The majority of Head Start participants attend preschools run by one of the 17,000 Head Start centers across the country. Some home-based services are also offered to support families.

Head Start is notable among early childhood education programs because it provides more than just free childcare and education. Head Start is required to serve at least two meals per day to the young children who attend these schools, as well as offer speech therapy and other kinds of developmental support and health services when needed.
In some rural communities, Head Start’s ability to bring dentists and doctors to centers has dramatically expanded healthcare access for entire towns or school districts.

Many states and cities have introduced or expanded their own free public preschool options in recent years. But Head Start continues to be an essential early childcare program for low-income children and their families across the country.
President Lyndon B. Johnson’s administration launched Head Start in 1965 as an eight-week summer preschool program.

Over 500,000 low-income children participated in Head Start during this first summer. The program quickly proved popular and effective. The government then expanded the program to cover the entire school year, starting in the fall of 1965.

The early childhood experts who designed Head Start understood that simply offering free education to low-income children was not enough to offset the impacts of growing up in poverty. They recognized the necessity of a comprehensive, whole-child approach, a philosophy that continues to define the program today.

So while Head Start primarily provides education and childcare services, the program also requires parents to participate in parent-child activities and other activities that engage families across their broader communities.

Since 1965, other programs have been introduced under the Head Start umbrella, including Early Head Start, which provides Head Start services to children from birth to 3 years old, as well as pregnant women.
Overall, more than 40 million children have participated in Head Start since its launch.
Head Start’s impact on children
Numerous studies have analyzed how Head Start affects children who participate in the program, as well as their families.

Much of the research has found that Head Start’s positive effects on its participants are sustained through the end of third grade. These effects include significantly improved educational and health outcomes.

Researchers have also found that participating in Head Start lowered the likelihood of being placed in special education or committing a crime, and it lowered child mortality rates, among other positive results.
Head Start’s longer-term impacts, meaning those measured over the course of a child’s lifetime, are less clear.

Some studies have found impacts that last well into adulthood, though some have not. These studies contribute to the debate over the benefits of Head Start “fading out” over time, though the causes and significance of this phenomenon are disputed.

One notable study that Congress commissioned in 2010 found positive effects for Head Start participants in cognitive, social-emotional and health outcomes, though few of these impacts lasted through the end of first grade.

Both the Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank, and the Trump administration have cited this report to argue that Head Start is ineffective. However, it is important to note that many scholars have pointed to significant problems with the methodology of the study.

The Trump administration suggests that these changes will cut costs by $1.5 billion to $3 billion by 2031. Those savings would account for roughly 0.04% of any given year’s typical total federal budget.

I believe that these proposed changes fly in the face of Head Start’s goals, and changes to Head Start’s rules and standards will likely contribute to the existing issues of inconsistent access to Head Start across the country.

The Administration for Children and Families, an office within the Department of Health and Human Services, is accepting public comments on the changes, as required by federal law. It will review the comments after the Oct. 6, 2026, deadline.
As of late September, there were over 18,465 comments, most expressing serious concern about these changes.

articles.title: Are religious charter schools constitutional? After deadlocked SCOTUS decision, another Oklahoma case is trying to find out
articles.author: Charles J. Russo, Joseph Panzer Chair in Education and Research Professor of Law, University of Dayton
paras: Just over a year ago, the U.S. Supreme Court rendered an unusual judgment: a tied vote.

Without stating why, Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself from Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board v. Drummond, a case about whether it would have been constitutional to open a Catholic charter school. The remaining justices deadlocked 4-4, leaving in place lower court rulings that blocked the school. Oklahoma courts agreed that allowing state funding to a religious school would have violated both Oklahoma law and the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution.

Now, a new contender is attempting to become America’s first religious charter school. On Sept. 24, 2026, a federal court judge allowed a suit to proceed from Ben Gamla, a Jewish organization whose application to participate in Oklahoma’s charter school program was denied earlier this year.

This yearslong controversy goes to the heart of questions about how much public aid is permissible to faith-based institutions under the First Amendment’s establishment clause, which forbids the government from making laws “respecting an establishment of religion.” More broadly, it reflects tensions over religion’s place in public life – while highlighting the Supreme Court’s increasingly friendly attitude toward faith-based schools.

Ben Gamla operates a network of secular charter schools in Florida that teach in Hebrew and English. Its application in Oklahoma proposes a school that would provide both secular and religious education.
The charter school movement began in earnest in the United States in 1991, starting in Minnesota. Forty-six states and the District of Columbia now permit them to operate.

Charter schools differ significantly from other public schools. Though funded with taxpayer money, they are typically run by private organizations, under charters that can be renewed or terminated depending on whether schools meet their stated goals. While free from many state laws and regulations about staff and curricula, charter schools remain subject to federal and local antidiscrimination laws.

Under Oklahoma’s Constitution, no public funds can support religious institutions. Historically, the U.S. Supreme Court also placed significant limits on aid to faith-based schools, although not as strict as those enforced by Oklahoma and some other states.

Under what is known as the “child benefit test,” the court allowed some forms of aid, such as laws reimbursing parents for the costs of transportation to school and lending textbooks for secular instruction, because the direct beneficiaries were students rather than their schools.
Three recent Supreme Court cases, though, loosened the restrictions on aid to faith-based schools and families.

The first, 2017’s Trinity Lutheran v. Comer, arose after a church preschool in Missouri was denied funds from a public program to improve playground safety. The court ruled that denying faith-based institutions generally available benefits for which they are otherwise qualified violates the First Amendment’s free exercise clause, which says the government cannot make a law “prohibiting the free exercise” of religion.

Excluding faith-based institutions and believers solely because they are religious “is odious to our Constitution,” the court emphasized. Trinity Lutheran ushered in a new era of its First Amendment jurisprudence by expanding the boundaries of permissible aid.

Three years later, in Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue, a dispute arose over a tax credit program for contributions to student scholarship organizations. The state constitution prohibits public aid to “sectarian” schools, so Montana did not allow families that received these scholarships to use them at religious schools.

The Supreme Court reasoned that using the scholarships at faith-based schools would be acceptable under the U.S. Constitution’s establishment clause. The majority concluded that Montana’s no-aid provision discriminated against people based on their beliefs. The court added that because Montana’s rule separated religion and state more strictly than the establishment clause, it was unconstitutional – a distinction that may prove important in the Ben Gamla case.

Finally, in 2022, the court took up Carson v. Makin, a case from Maine. The justices invalidated Maine’s attempt to exclude faith-based schools from a program providing tuition assistance to families who lived in areas without their own public schools. The court reasoned that Maine’s program violated the free exercise clause because it was not “neutral” toward religion: It impermissibly excluded otherwise eligible institutions and families solely because they were religious.

Returning to Oklahoma, the September 2026 ruling found that Ben Gamla had standing to pursue its claim that state officials violated the organization’s First Amendment rights to free exercise of religion.

However, Judge David L. Russell’s order does not resolve the underlying issue of religious charter schools once and for all. Rather, it allows the school’s application to proceed while the court considers the underling constitutional questions. Meanwhile, Oklahoma has 30 days to appeal the judgment to the 10th Circuit.

Coming on the heels of the Catholic charter school case, Ben Gamla might seem, as New York Yankees baseball great Yogi Berra once said, like a case of “déjà vu all over again.” Yet the litigation over Ben Gamla is different from the previous case involving St. Isidore of Seville Catholic Virtual School.

In 2024, when the Supreme Court of Oklahoma refused to let the state open St. Isidore, the justices primarily relied on the state constitution’s prohibition against using public money to benefit or support any religious institution.

In Ben Gamla, though, the trial court judge relied on federal case law. I believe this strengthens the chances that this case may make its way to the Supreme Court – and perhaps achieve a different outcome. In fact, Russell specifically cited the three recent Supreme Court decisions, among others, as supporting Ben Gamla’s argument that the U.S. Constitution permits aid to faith-based schools.

Russell emphasized that his order “does not express a judgment on the wisdom on the State of Oklahoma opening up its coffers to charter schools of disparate philosophical or educational provisions.” Having done so, however, state officials cannot “single out religious schools for exclusion solely because of their religious character.”

Ben Gamla may turn out to be the next step in the Supreme Court’s increasingly friendly approach to the important question of state aid to faith-based schools, their students and their parents. How this dispute plays out will tell us not only about the court’s thinking, but why supporters on both sides have such different visions over religion’s role – if any – in American education and public life.
